items: Part A is 30 of 200 marks: answer 15 of 20, 2 marks each, −0.5 per wrong answer.
Do it last or first, but cap it at 30–35 minutes; skip any puzzle that has no clear route in 60 seconds.
Daily 20 minutes of mixed PYQs keeps speed up; log every slip by type (arithmetic, misread, logic).

Tables, bar charts and pie charts

Numerical ability: Successive changes of a% and b% give a net change of a + b + ab/100 %.
If A finishes a job in a days and B in b days, together they take ab/(a + b) days.
Average speed over two equal distances at x and y is 2xy/(x + y), not (x + y)/2.
For 2 years, compound minus simple interest = P(r/100)².
nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!); n people around a circle can sit in (n − 1)! ways.
Geometry, mensuration and data interpret: Circle: area πr², circumference 2πr; sphere: volume 4/3 πr³, surface 4πr².
Cylinder volume πr²h; cone volume πr²h/3 (one third of the cylinder).
Doubling every length multiplies area by 4 and volume by 8.
On a log axis equal distances mean equal ratios, not equal differences.
Logical reasoning and puzzles: In a number series check differences first, then ratios, then alternate terms.
'Some A are B' never implies 'Some A are not B'.
Direction problems: track net east–west and north–south moves; distance = √(x² + y²).
In arrangement puzzles place the most constrained person first, then branch.
Statistics and analytical aptitude: Adding c to every value shifts the mean by c and leaves the SD unchanged.
Multiplying every value by k multiplies mean and SD by k and the variance by k².
Clock-hand angle = |30H − 5.5M| degrees; the hands overlap every 720/11 ≈ 65.45 min.
An ordinary year moves the weekday on by 1, a leap year by 2.

items: Highest-yield unit for both Part B and Part C: enzyme kinetics, thermodynamics and metabolism appear every session.
Learn numbers that turn into calculations: ΔG°′ values, pKa values, P/O ratios, Km/Vmax shifts with inhibitors.
Pair every metabolic pathway with its microbial version (fermentations, glyoxylate cycle, Entner–Doudoroff).
Part C here is graph reading: Lineweaver–Burk plots, titration curves and O₂-binding curves.

Atoms, bonds and stabilising interaction: Hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces
pH, buffers and biophysical chemistry: pH, pKa and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
Thermodynamics and bioenergetics: Laws of thermodynamics in living cells
Free energy, ΔG°′ and equilibrium constants
Carbohydrates and lipids: Starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin and peptidoglycan
Protein function: oxygen binding and all: Ligand binding: Kd and fractional saturation
Enzymes and enzyme kinetics: Regulation: allostery, covalent modification, zymogens, isozymes

Atoms, bonds and stabilising interaction: A C–C covalent bond is about 348 kJ/mol; an H-bond 4–20 kJ/mol; a van der Waals contact 0.4–4 kJ/mol.
An optimal H-bond has a donor–acceptor distance of about 2.8–3.0 Å and is nearly linear.
The hydrophobic effect is entropy-driven: ordered water around non-polar groups is released.
Electrostatic force falls with dielectric constant: water ≈ 80, a protein interior ≈ 4, so salt bridges are stronger when buried.
pH, buffers and biophysical chemistry: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]); a buffer works best within pKa ± 1.
Blood is buffered by HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃ (pKa 6.1) and the cytosol by phosphate (pKa₂ 6.86).
For an amino acid without an ionisable side chain, pI = (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2; glycine ≈ 5.97.
Osmotic pressure π = iMRT; colligative properties depend on particle number, not identity.
First-order half-life t½ = 0.693/k and does not depend on the starting concentration.
Thermodynamics and bioenergetics: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q and ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq: each tenfold change in K′eq is 5.7 kJ/mol at 25 °C.
ATP hydrolysis: ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol, but about −50 to −65 kJ/mol under cellular conditions.
PEP (−61.9) and 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (−49.3 kJ/mol) rank above ATP, so they drive substrate-level phosphorylation.
ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′ with F = 96.5 kJ V⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Carbohydrates and lipids: Glucose and galactose are C-4 epimers; glucose and mannose are C-2 epimers.
Sucrose, Glc(α1↔2β)Fru, is non-reducing; lactose, Gal(β1→4)Glc, is reducing.
Cellulose is β1→4 glucose; amylose α1→4; glycogen branches α1→6 every 8–12 residues.
Peptidoglycan: NAG–NAM chains (β1→4) cross-linked by peptides; lysozyme cuts the NAM–NAG bond.
Cis double bonds lower the melting point; linoleic acid (18:2 cis-Δ9,12) is essential in humans.
Amino acids, proteins and vitamins: The peptide bond is planar, with about 40% double-bond character, and almost always trans.
Absorbance at 280 nm comes mainly from Trp and Tyr.
Coenzymes: B1 → TPP, B2 → FAD/FMN, B3 → NAD(P), B5 → CoA, B6 → PLP, B7 → biotin (carboxylations), B12 → cobalamin.
Vitamin K is needed to γ-carboxylate glutamate in clotting factors II, VII, IX and X.
Selenocysteine, the 21st amino acid, is encoded by UGA plus a SECIS element.
Protein conformation and stability: α-helix: 3.6 residues per turn, 5.4 Å pitch, 1.5 Å rise per residue; C=O of residue n bonds to N–H of n + 4.
Right-handed α-helix sits near φ −57°, ψ −47°; β-sheet near φ −120°, ψ +120°; only glycine readily reaches the left-handed region.
Proline breaks helices; glycine and proline are common in β-turns.
Anfinsen’s RNase A experiment: sequence determines structure (refolding after urea and β-mercaptoethanol are removed).
GroEL/GroES is a chaperonin; Hsp70 binds exposed hydrophobic segments.
Protein function: oxygen binding and all: Myoglobin binds O₂ hyperbolically (P50 ≈ 0.26 kPa); haemoglobin sigmoidally (P50 ≈ 3.5 kPa, Hill n ≈ 3).
Bohr effect: lower pH and higher CO₂ lower O₂ affinity and shift the curve right.
2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of deoxy-Hb; fetal Hb (γ chains) binds it weakly, so it holds O₂ more tightly.
CO binds haemoglobin about 250 times more tightly than O₂.
Fractional saturation θ = [L]/([L] + Kd); θ = 0.5 when [L] = Kd.
Enzymes and enzyme kinetics: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); when [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2.
Competitive inhibitor: apparent Km rises, Vmax unchanged. Uncompetitive: both fall. Pure non-competitive: Vmax falls, Km unchanged.
Diffusion-limited enzymes reach kcat/Km ≈ 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ (triose phosphate isomerase, catalase).
Chymotrypsin’s triad is Ser195, His57, Asp102; it cuts after Phe, Trp and Tyr.
Lactate dehydrogenase has five isozymes built from H and M subunits.
Nucleic acid conformation and stability: B-DNA: right-handed, about 10.5 bp per turn, 3.4 Å rise, 20 Å wide. A-DNA: 11 bp per turn. Z-DNA: left-handed, 12 bp per turn.
Tm rises with GC content and ionic strength; single strands absorb about 40% more at 260 nm (hyperchromic effect).
Pure DNA has A260/A280 ≈ 1.8; pure RNA ≈ 2.0.
Lk = Tw + Wr; type I topoisomerases change Lk by 1, type II (gyrase) by 2.
tRNA has a cloverleaf secondary and L-shaped tertiary structure ending in 3′-CCA.
Glycolysis, TCA cycle and oxidative phos: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose; control points are hexokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase.
PFK-1 is activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, inhibited by ATP and citrate.
One TCA turn gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP (or ATP) and 2 CO₂.
P/O ratios are about 2.5 for NADH and 1.5 for succinate (FADH₂): roughly 30–32 ATP per glucose.
Inhibitors: rotenone (complex I), antimycin A (III), cyanide and CO (IV), oligomycin (ATP synthase); DNP uncouples.
Carbohydrate and lipid metabolism: Gluconeogenesis bypasses: pyruvate carboxylase + PEPCK, FBPase-1, glucose-6-phosphatase; it costs 4 ATP + 2 GTP per glucose.
The oxidative pentose phosphate phase gives 2 NADPH per glucose-6-phosphate; G6PD is rate-limiting.
Entner–Doudoroff (e.g., Pseudomonas, Zymomonas) yields 1 ATP, 1 NADH and 1 NADPH per glucose.
Palmitate β-oxidation: 7 cycles → 8 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH₂, 7 NADH, net 106 ATP.
The glyoxylate cycle (isocitrate lyase, malate synthase) lets bacteria and plants grow on acetate.
Amino acid and nucleotide metabolism: Aminotransferases need PLP; ALT and AST are clinical liver markers.
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (activated by N-acetylglutamate) is the urea cycle’s control step; each urea costs 4 high-energy bonds.
The purine ring is built on PRPP; the pyrimidine ring is made first and then attached to PRPP.
Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; 5-fluorouracil (as FdUMP) inhibits thymidylate synthase.
Sulfonamides block bacterial folate synthesis as PABA analogues; trimethoprim blocks bacterial DHFR.

topics: Cell walls and bacterial surface structures
Microbial physiology: growth, stress and AMR

items: Treat prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell structure side by side: envelopes, transport, division and cytoskeleton.
The revised syllabus adds microbial physiology (growth kinetics, stress responses, AMR): high value for a microbiology candidate.
Part C favours experiments: drug effects on transport, membrane potentials, cell-cycle arrest points.
Memorise signal sequences and the destinations they encode.

Membrane structure and model membranes: Bacterial, archaeal and eukaryotic membranes compared
Membrane transport and electrical proper: P-, V-, F-type and ABC pumps
Ion channels and the Nernst equation
Cell walls and bacterial surface structu: Gram-positive wall: peptidoglycan and teichoic acids
Gram-negative envelope: outer membrane, LPS, porins, periplasm
Nucleus and intracellular organelles: Nuclear envelope and nuclear pore complex
Protein sorting and membrane traffic: Endocytosis, exocytosis and bacterial secretion systems

Cell division and cell cycle: Bacterial binary fission and the Z-ring
Microbial physiology: growth, stress and: Stress responses: heat shock, SOS, stringent, sporulation

Membrane structure and model membranes: Archaeal lipids are isoprenoid chains ether-linked to glycerol-1-phosphate; tetraether lipids form monolayers.
Hopanoids act as sterol substitutes in many bacterial membranes.
Phosphatidylserine faces the cytosol; its exposure on the outer leaflet marks apoptotic cells.
A transmembrane α-helix needs about 20 hydrophobic residues to span ~30 Å.
Cold-shifted cells raise their proportion of unsaturated and short fatty acids (homeoviscous adaptation).
Membrane transport and electrical proper: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP; it is P-type (phosphorylated Asp).
Nernst: E = (61.5/z) log(Co/Ci) mV at 37 °C; a typical resting potential is about −70 mV.
The bacterial PEP:sugar phosphotransferase system phosphorylates sugars as it imports them (group translocation).
Aquaporins pass water but block H₃O⁺ (NPA motifs).
ABC transporters import nutrients in bacteria and export drugs in eukaryotes (P-glycoprotein/MDR1).
Cell walls and bacterial surface structu: Gram-positive peptidoglycan is 20–80 nm thick; Gram-negative is 2–7 nm under an outer membrane.
LPS = lipid A (endotoxin) + core polysaccharide + O-antigen.
Mycoplasmas lack a wall, carry sterols in their membrane and are resistant to penicillin.
The bacterial flagellum is driven by proton-motive force; the eukaryotic flagellum by dynein ATPase on a 9 + 2 axoneme.
Fungal walls are chitin and glucans; plant primary walls are cellulose microfibrils in hemicellulose and pectin.
Nucleus and intracellular organelles: Nuclear import uses an NLS (SV40 T antigen: PKKKRKV), importins and a Ran-GTP gradient that is high in the nucleus.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have 70S ribosomes, circular DNA and double membranes: evidence for endosymbiosis.
Lysosomal enzymes get mannose-6-phosphate in the cis-Golgi; losing it causes I-cell disease.
Peroxisomes hold catalase and β-oxidise very-long-chain fatty acids; failure causes Zellweger syndrome.
Plastids: proplastid, chloroplast, chromoplast, amyloplast, etioplast.
Protein sorting and membrane traffic: SRP binds the signal peptide and pauses translation until it docks with its receptor at the Sec61 translocon.
KDEL retrieves soluble ER proteins; COPII carries cargo ER → Golgi, COPI Golgi → ER.
Clathrin, adaptors and dynamin form endocytic vesicles; the LDL receptor is the classic example.
Bacterial secretion: Sec (unfolded), Tat (folded) and Types I–VII; Type III is the injectisome of Salmonella and Yersinia.
Cytoskeleton and motility: Microtubules: 13 protofilaments of α/β-tubulin, 25 nm wide; actin filaments 7 nm; intermediate filaments about 10 nm.
Kinesins mostly walk to the plus end; dyneins to the minus end.
Colchicine and nocodazole depolymerise microtubules; taxol stabilises them; cytochalasin blocks actin polymerisation; phalloidin stabilises F-actin.
FtsZ (tubulin homologue) forms the Z-ring; MreB (actin homologue) keeps rods rod-shaped; crescentin is intermediate-filament-like.
Organisation of genes and chromosomes: The nucleosome core wraps 147 bp around an H2A, H2B, H3, H4 octamer; H1 binds linker DNA.
Constitutive heterochromatin (centromeres, telomeres) is rich in satellite DNA and H3K9me3.
C-value paradox: genome size does not track organismal complexity.
In Cot curves highly repetitive DNA reanneals first.
Bacterial IS elements carry only transposase; composite transposons (Tn5, Tn10) carry drug-resistance genes between IS copies.
Cell division and cell cycle: At G1/S, cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb and releases E2F.
The spindle checkpoint holds APC/C–Cdc20 until every kinetochore is attached.
Meiosis I is reductional; synapsis at zygotene, crossing over at pachytene, chiasmata visible at diplotene.
E. coli: C period (replication) ~40 min + D period ~20 min; overlapping rounds of replication allow 20-minute doublings.
Caulobacter divides asymmetrically into a stalked and a swarmer cell; Streptomyces forms spores by fragmenting hyphae.
Apoptosis, necrosis and autophagy: Cytochrome c, Apaf-1 and procaspase-9 form the apoptosome.
Fas and TNF receptors recruit FADD and activate caspase-8.
Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL block apoptosis; Bax and Bak permeabilise the mitochondrial outer membrane.
Necrosis swells and bursts cells (inflammation); apoptosis blebs them and ladders DNA in ~180 bp steps.
mTOR inhibits autophagy; lipidated LC3 (Atg8) marks autophagosomes.
Microbial physiology: growth, stress and: Generations n = (log N − log N₀)/0.301; generation time g = t/n.
Stringent response: RelA makes (p)ppGpp during amino-acid starvation and shuts down rRNA synthesis.
Bacillus sporulation is driven by Spo0A~P and a sigma cascade (σF, σE, σG, σK).
Resistance mechanisms: drug inactivation (β-lactamases), target change (PBP2a from mecA in MRSA), efflux pumps, reduced porin entry.
Persisters are dormant, drug-tolerant cells, not genetically resistant mutants.

topics: Gene regulation in bacteria and phages
Gene regulation in eukaryotes and viruses

items: The core of molecular biology: replication, repair, transcription, translation and gene regulation.
Learn the bacterial version first (E. coli, λ, lac, trp), then the eukaryotic differences.
Antibiotic and inhibitor targets are favourite one-liners; make a single table of them.
Part C uses classic experiments: Meselson–Stahl, lac merodiploids, attenuation mutants.

DNA replication in bacteria: DNA polymerases I, II and III
Leading and lagging strands, Okazaki fragments
Eukaryotic replication, telomeres and pl: Roles of Pol α, δ and ε
Plasmid replication: theta and rolling circle
DNA damage and repair: Double-strand break repair and the SOS response
Transcription in bacteria: RNA polymerase core enzyme and σ factors
Eukaryotic transcription and RNA process: RNA polymerases I, II and III
General transcription factors and the TATA box
Protein processing, targeting and degrad: Targeting to mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes
Gene regulation in bacteria and phages: The lac operon: negative and positive control
Gene regulation in eukaryotes and viruse: Viral gene regulation (HIV Tat, adenovirus E1A)
Epigenetics and gene silencing: Bacterial epigenetics: Dam methylation and phase variation

DNA replication in bacteria: Pol III holoenzyme copies about 1000 nt/s with high processivity; its ε subunit proofreads 3′→5′.
Pol I removes RNA primers with its 5′→3′ exonuclease; the Klenow fragment lacks that activity.
DnaB is the helicase, DnaG the primase; SSB coats single strands and gyrase relieves supercoils ahead of the fork.
With proofreading and mismatch repair the error rate is about 10⁻⁹–10⁻¹⁰ per base.
Meselson and Stahl used ¹⁵N/¹⁴N and CsCl density gradients (1958).
Eukaryotic replication, telomeres and pl: MCM is loaded in G1 (licensing) and fired by CDK and DDK in S, so DNA replicates only once per cycle.
Pol ε makes the leading strand, Pol δ the lagging strand; Pol α–primase starts each fragment.
Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase with its own RNA template (TTAGGG repeats in vertebrates).
ColE1 copy number is set by antisense RNA I pairing with RNA II, helped by Rop.
Rolling-circle replication is used by ϕX174, M13 and many small Gram-positive plasmids.
DNA damage and repair: UV makes cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts; nucleotide excision repair (UvrABC) removes them.
E. coli mismatch repair: MutS finds the mismatch, MutL links, MutH nicks the unmethylated GATC on the new strand.
SOS: activated RecA triggers LexA self-cleavage and induces error-prone Pol V (UmuD′₂C).
Double-strand breaks: non-homologous end joining (Ku70/80, error-prone) or homologous recombination (accurate, needs a template).
Xeroderma pigmentosum is an NER defect; Lynch syndrome a mismatch-repair defect.
Homologous and site-specific recombinati: Chi (5′-GCTGGTGG-3′) switches RecBCD from nuclease to RecA loader.
RuvAB drives branch migration; RuvC cuts Holliday junctions.
Site-specific recombination: λ integrase (attP × attB), Cre/loxP, Hin inversion for Salmonella flagellar phase variation.
Transposition is cut-and-paste (Tn5, Tn10) or replicative (Tn3) and leaves short target-site duplications.
Transcription in bacteria: E. coli core polymerase is α₂ββ′ω; σ⁷⁰ reads −35 TTGACA and −10 TATAAT.
Intrinsic terminator: GC-rich hairpin then a U-tract; Rho is an ATP-dependent helicase that loads at rut sites.
Rifampicin binds the β subunit and blocks initiation; actinomycin D intercalates into DNA.
Alternative sigma factors: σ³² heat shock, σ⁵⁴ nitrogen, σˢ stationary phase, σ²⁸ flagella.
Eukaryotic transcription and RNA process: Pol I makes 28S/18S/5.8S rRNA; Pol II mRNA and most snRNAs and miRNAs; Pol III tRNA, 5S rRNA and U6.
TFIID (TBP) binds TATA; TFIIH unwinds DNA and phosphorylates CTD Ser5.
The 5′ cap is m⁷G joined 5′–5′ by a triphosphate; the poly(A) signal is AAUAAA.
The spliceosome uses U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6 snRNPs; the branch-point A forms a lariat.
α-Amanitin blocks Pol II strongly, Pol III weakly and Pol I not at all.
Translation: Bacterial initiation: the Shine–Dalgarno sequence (AGGAGG) pairs with the 3′ end of 16S rRNA; the first tRNA carries fMet.
Peptidyl transferase is 23S rRNA: the ribosome is a ribozyme.
30S drugs: aminoglycosides, tetracyclines. 50S drugs: chloramphenicol, macrolides, linezolid. Puromycin causes premature release.
Wobble allows G·U pairs and inosine at anticodon position 34.
Protein processing, targeting and degrad: N-linked glycosylation on Asn-X-Ser/Thr starts co-translationally in the ER.
K48-linked polyubiquitin sends proteins to the 26S proteasome via an E1 → E2 → E3 cascade.
The N-end rule: the N-terminal residue sets a protein’s half-life.
Mitochondrial matrix proteins carry an amphipathic N-terminal presequence and pass through TOM and TIM.
Gene regulation in bacteria and phages: lac: LacI binds the operator; allolactose induces; CAP–cAMP activates when glucose is low (catabolite repression).
trp attenuation: ribosome stalling at Trp codons in the leader decides between the antiterminator (2:3) and terminator (3:4) hairpins.
λ: CI repressor maintains lysogeny, Cro drives lysis; high CII (poor nutrients, high MOI) favours lysogeny.
lacI⁻ and Oᶜ mutants are constitutive; merodiploids show Oᶜ acts only in cis, lacI⁺ in trans.
Gene regulation in eukaryotes and viruse: Histone acetylation (HATs) opens chromatin, HDACs close it; H3K4me3 marks active promoters, H3K27me3 Polycomb silencing.
CpG methylation silences promoters; DNMT1 maintains methylation, DNMT3a/b set it de novo.
miRNA pathway: pri-miRNA → Drosha → exportin-5 → Dicer → RISC (Argonaute).
HIV Tat binds TAR RNA and recruits P-TEFb to boost elongation.
Yeast GAL4 has separable DNA-binding and activation domains, the basis of the two-hybrid assay.
Epigenetics and gene silencing: XIST lncRNA coats the X to be inactivated; Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes − 1.
Position-effect variegation: the Drosophila white gene silenced next to heterochromatin.
Imprinted Igf2 is expressed from the paternal allele, H19 from the maternal.
Dam methylation of GATC times replication (SeqA) and guides mismatch repair.
E. coli Pap pili switch on and off through Dam methylation and Lrp (phase variation).

Signalling questions test pathway order and what a mutation or drug does at each step.
Learn the TLR–ligand table, antibody classes, MHC pathways and the four hypersensitivity types until you can write them blind.

Receptors, GPCRs and second messengers: GPCRs have seven transmembrane helices; Gα-GTP activates effectors until its own GTPase switches it off.
Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gsα and locks it on (cAMP rises); pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Giα and blocks inhibition.
PLCβ cuts PIP₂ into IP₃ (releases ER Ca²⁺) and DAG (activates PKC).
Steroid hormones bind intracellular nuclear receptors that act as transcription factors.
Enzyme-linked receptors and developmenta: RTK autophosphorylation → Grb2 (SH2) → SOS (GEF) → Ras-GTP → Raf → MEK → ERK.
Oncogenic Ras mutations (G12, G13, Q61) keep Ras GTP-bound.
Without Wnt, β-catenin is phosphorylated by GSK3 in the APC–Axin complex and degraded.
Notch is cut by γ-secretase and its intracellular domain enters the nucleus.
Two-component systems, chemotaxis and qu: The sensor kinase autophosphorylates on His and passes the phosphate to an Asp on the response regulator (EnvZ–OmpR).
CheY~P binds the flagellar motor → clockwise rotation → tumble; CheR/CheB methylation gives adaptation.
Vibrio fischeri LuxI makes acyl-homoserine lactone; LuxR–AHL switches on the lux genes.
Staphylococcus aureus agr uses autoinducing peptides; Bacillus subtilis competence uses ComX.
Active phytochrome (Pfr) enters the nucleus and triggers degradation of PIF transcription factors.
Cell adhesion, junctions and neurotransm: Cadherins need Ca²⁺; integrins are α/β dimers that bind RGD motifs in fibronectin.
A gap-junction connexon is six connexins and passes molecules under about 1 kDa.
Acetylcholinesterase ends cholinergic signals; organophosphates inhibit it.
Erythropoietin from the kidney drives red-cell production; G-CSF neutrophils; thrombopoietin platelets.
Innate immunity: TLR4 senses LPS (with MD-2, CD14); TLR2 lipoproteins; TLR3 dsRNA; TLR5 flagellin; TLR7/8 ssRNA; TLR9 unmethylated CpG DNA.
Most TLRs signal through MyD88 to NF-κB; TLR3 uses TRIF only.
Type I interferons (α, β) induce an antiviral state via JAK–STAT; IFN-γ (type II) activates macrophages.
NK cells kill cells with low MHC I (missing self) using perforin and granzymes.
Antigens, antibodies and antibody divers: IgG (~150 kDa) crosses the placenta; IgM is a pentamer and the first antibody made; secretory IgA is a dimer; IgE arms mast cells.
RAG1/RAG2 cut at recombination signal sequences following the 12/23 rule; TdT adds N-nucleotides.
Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) drives both somatic hypermutation and class switching.
Hybridomas: B cell × myeloma fused with PEG, selected in HAT medium because the myeloma is HGPRT⁻.
A hapten is antigenic but not immunogenic until coupled to a carrier protein.
MHC, antigen presentation and lymphocyte: MHC I (all nucleated cells) shows 8–10-residue peptides to CD8⁺ T cells; MHC II (APCs) shows 13–25-residue peptides to CD4⁺ T cells.
TAP pumps proteasome peptides into the ER; CLIP holds the MHC II groove until HLA-DM swaps in peptide.
Co-stimulation: CD28 on the T cell binds B7 (CD80/86); CTLA-4 competes and inhibits.
Th1 (IFN-γ, T-bet), Th2 (IL-4, GATA3), Th17 (IL-17, RORγt), Treg (FoxP3, IL-10, TGF-β).
Complement and effector responses: The classical pathway starts with C1q on bound IgM or IgG; C3 convertases are C4b2a (classical, lectin) and C3bBb (alternative).
C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins; C3b opsonises; C5b–9 forms the membrane attack complex.
Secondary responses are faster and larger, mainly IgG, and of higher affinity.
CD55 (DAF) and CD59 protect host cells; their loss causes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.
Hypersensitivity, autoimmunity and immun: Type I: IgE and mast cells (anaphylaxis). II: antibody against cell surfaces (haemolytic disease of the newborn). III: immune complexes (serum sickness, SLE). IV: delayed T-cell (tuberculin test).
AIRE drives thymic expression of tissue antigens for negative selection.
SCID: ADA deficiency or common γ-chain (IL2RG) defects; Bruton’s X-linked agammaglobulinaemia: BTK mutation, no B cells.
HIV binds CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4; AIDS is defined by CD4 counts below 200 cells/µL.
Immunity to infection and vaccines: Extracellular bacteria are cleared by antibody and complement; Mycobacterium tuberculosis needs Th1, IFN-γ and granulomas.
Helminths drive Th2 responses, IgE and eosinophils.
Evasion: antigenic variation (trypanosome VSG), capsules, protein A binding IgG Fc, viral down-regulation of MHC I.
Conjugate vaccines (Hib, pneumococcal) link polysaccharide to protein to recruit T-cell help.
Alum is the classic adjuvant; BCG is live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis.
Host–pathogen interaction: Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates EF-2; botulinum and tetanus toxins are zinc proteases that cut SNAREs.
Listeria uses ActA to polymerise host actin; Salmonella’s SPI-1 type III system triggers membrane ruffling and uptake.
Plant PTI is triggered by PAMPs (flg22 via FLS2); ETI by R-protein recognition of effectors, often with a hypersensitive response.
Agrobacterium transfers T-DNA through its VirB/D4 type IV system and causes crown gall.
Influenza haemagglutinin binds sialic acid; low endosomal pH triggers membrane fusion.
Cancer: Knudson’s two-hit hypothesis came from retinoblastoma (RB1).
p53 induces p21 (G1 arrest) and apoptosis; it is mutated in about half of human cancers.
HPV E6 degrades p53 and E7 inactivates Rb; EBV, HBV, HTLV-1 and KSHV are also human tumour viruses.
The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) makes BCR–ABL, the target of imatinib.
Epithelial–mesenchymal transition and matrix metalloproteinases drive invasion.

Draw each gene hierarchy once; Part C asks what a loss-of-function mutant looks like.

Basic concepts of development: Totipotent (zygote) → pluripotent (inner cell mass, ES cells) → multipotent → unipotent.
The Spemann–Mangold organiser (dorsal blastopore lip) induces a second body axis when grafted.
Genomic equivalence was shown by nuclear transfer: Gurdon’s frogs and Dolly the sheep (1996).
Yamanaka factors Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc reprogram fibroblasts into iPS cells.
Gametogenesis, fertilisation and early d: Sea urchin: fast block by membrane depolarisation, slow block by the cortical granule reaction.
Mouse sperm bind the zona pellucida glycoproteins (ZP2/ZP3).
Cleavage is holoblastic in sea urchins and mammals, meroblastic discoidal in birds and fish.
The mammalian blastocyst is an inner cell mass plus trophectoderm.
Axes and pattern formation in Drosophila: bicoid mRNA is anterior, nanos posterior; Nanos represses hunchback translation.
Cascade: maternal → gap → pair-rule (even-skipped, fushi tarazu: 7 stripes) → segment polarity (engrailed, wingless) → Hox.
Hox genes show colinearity: 3′ genes act more anteriorly and earlier.
Hensen’s node is the chick equivalent of the organiser.
Organogenesis, sex determination and met: Vulva: anchor-cell LIN-3 (EGF) → LET-23 in P6.p (1° fate); lateral LIN-12 (Notch) gives 2° fates.
Limb: the AER (FGF8) drives proximal–distal outgrowth; the ZPA (Shh) sets the anterior–posterior axis.
Mammals: SRY on the Y makes testes; Drosophila: X:A ratio acting through Sex-lethal.
Amphibian metamorphosis needs thyroid hormone (T3); insect moulting needs ecdysone, with juvenile hormone setting larval vs adult.
Plant development: The Polygonum-type embryo sac has 7 cells and 8 nuclei; the endosperm is triploid.
The shoot meristem is kept by WUSCHEL–CLAVATA3 feedback.
ABC model: A sepals, A + B petals, B + C stamens, C carpels (AP1; AP3/PI; AG); E-class SEP genes are needed for all four.
Florigen is the FT protein moving through the phloem; CONSTANS senses long days in Arabidopsis.
Programmed cell death, ageing and senesc: In C. elegans 131 somatic cells die by programmed cell death: ced-3 (caspase), ced-4 (Apaf-1-like), ced-9 (Bcl-2-like).
The plant hypersensitive response is local cell death that walls off biotrophic pathogens.
Telomere shortening sets the Hayflick limit of about 50 divisions in human fibroblasts.
Cytokinin delays leaf senescence; ethylene and ABA promote it.

items: Lighter weighting: photosynthesis, nitrogen metabolism and hormones carry most of the marks.
Nitrogen fixation and plant–microbe signalling link straight to your microbiology focus.
Part C uses spectra and mutant phenotypes: action spectra, phytochrome red/far-red reversals, hormone-insensitive mutants.

Plant hormones: Brassinosteroids, jasmonates, salicylic acid and strigolactones

Photosynthesis: light reactions: P680 (PSII) splits water at the Mn₄CaO₅ cluster; PSI’s reaction centre is P700.
About 8 photons are needed per O₂; Emerson enhancement revealed two photosystems.
Cyclic electron flow around PSI makes ATP without NADPH.
The xanthophyll cycle (violaxanthin → zeaxanthin) dissipates excess light as heat.
Carbon fixation: C3, C4 and CAM: The Calvin cycle uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂ fixed.
Rubisco also adds O₂ to RuBP, starting photorespiration across chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion.
C4: PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ in mesophyll; decarboxylation in bundle-sheath cells concentrates CO₂ for Rubisco.
CAM plants open stomata at night and store malic acid in the vacuole.
Respiration and nitrogen metabolism: Alternative oxidase bypasses complexes III and IV; it heats the Arum spadix.
Nitrate reductase (cytosol) → nitrite reductase (plastid) → NH₄⁺ → glutamine synthetase–GOGAT.
Nitrogenase: N₂ + 8H⁺ + 8e⁻ + 16 ATP → 2NH₃ + H₂; it is destroyed by O₂.
Leghaemoglobin keeps nodule O₂ low; Nod factors are lipochitooligosaccharides from rhizobia.
Plant hormones: Auxin (IAA, made from Trp) binds the TIR1 F-box receptor and triggers degradation of Aux/IAA repressors.
Gibberellin bound to GID1 triggers degradation of DELLA repressors.
Ethylene is made from methionine via ACC synthase and ACC oxidase; its receptor ETR1 sits in the ER.
ABA closes stomata via PYR/PYL receptors, PP2C inhibition and SnRK2 activation.
Cytokinin signals through a His-kinase phosphorelay, like a bacterial two-component system.
Sensory photobiology and stomata: Pr absorbs red (~660 nm) and becomes Pfr; Pfr absorbs far-red (~730 nm) and reverts.
Phototropins (blue light) drive phototropism and stomatal opening.
Short-day plants measure night length: a red flash mid-night stops flowering, far-red after it restores flowering.
Stomata open when the H⁺-ATPase drives K⁺ uptake and water follows into guard cells.
Water, solute transport and phloem trans: Ψw = Ψs + Ψp (+ Ψg); pure water at atmospheric pressure is 0 MPa.
The Casparian strip of the endodermis forces water and ions into the symplast.
Münch pressure flow: sucrose loading at sources raises turgor and drives bulk flow to sinks.
Cucurbits load by polymer trapping (raffinose, stachyose).
Secondary metabolites and stress physiol: Terpenes come from IPP (C5) via the mevalonate (cytosol) or MEP (plastid) pathway.
Phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL) is the entry enzyme for lignin and flavonoids.
Proline and glycine betaine protect cells against osmotic stress.
Salicylic acid drives systemic acquired resistance; jasmonate drives defence against herbivores and necrotrophs.

Blood, haemostasis and the heart: Red cells live about 120 days; normal Hb is about 15 g/dL in men.
Group O is the universal red-cell donor, AB the universal recipient; Rh incompatibility causes haemolytic disease of the newborn.
Intrinsic (XII) and extrinsic (tissue factor–VII) pathways meet at factor X; thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin.
ECG: P = atrial depolarisation, QRS = ventricular depolarisation, T = ventricular repolarisation.
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate ≈ 5 L/min at rest.
Respiration and gas transport: Tidal volume is about 500 mL; vital capacity about 4.6 L.
About 70% of CO₂ travels as HCO₃⁻ (carbonic anhydrase, chloride shift).
Central chemoreceptors respond to H⁺/CO₂; carotid bodies to low O₂.
Fish gills use counter-current exchange; birds get one-way airflow through air sacs.
Nervous system and sense organs: Na⁺ influx depolarises and K⁺ efflux repolarises; tetrodotoxin blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.
Myelin gives saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.
Light: 11-cis → all-trans retinal → transducin → PDE → cGMP falls → rod hyperpolarises.
Cochlea: high frequencies at the base, low at the apex.
Excretion, osmoregulation and acid–base: GFR is about 125 mL/min (180 L/day); inulin clearance measures it.
The descending limb is water-permeable; the thick ascending limb pumps NaCl but is water-tight.
ADH inserts aquaporin-2 into collecting-duct cells.
Fish are ammonotelic, mammals ureotelic, birds and reptiles uricotelic.
Digestion, thermoregulation and stress: SGLT1 takes up glucose with Na⁺; GLUT5 takes up fructose.
BMR is about 60–70% of daily energy use in sedentary adults.
The hypothalamus is the thermostat; brown-fat UCP1 gives non-shivering heat.
Stress runs through the HPA axis (CRH → ACTH → cortisol) and the sympathoadrenal system (adrenaline).
Endocrinology and reproduction: The LH surge triggers ovulation around day 14.
Insulin acts through a receptor tyrosine kinase; glucagon through a GPCR and cAMP.
T4 is converted by deiodinases into the more active T3.
Peptide hormones use surface receptors; steroid and thyroid hormones use nuclear receptors.
Gut microbiome, holobionts and energy ho: The human gut is dominated by Bacillota (Firmicutes) and Bacteroidota (Bacteroidetes); bacterial cells roughly equal human cells (~10¹³).
Gut microbes ferment fibre into acetate, propionate and butyrate; butyrate feeds colonocytes.
16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (often V3–V4) gives composition; shotgun metagenomics gives functions.
Leptin from fat signals satiety; ghrelin from the stomach signals hunger.
Clostridioides difficile infection follows antibiotic dysbiosis; faecal microbiota transplant treats recurrences.

items: High-value for microbiology: bacterial gene transfer (transformation, conjugation, transduction) and phage genetics come up every session.
Most Part C questions are numerical: map distances, interference, LOD, Hardy–Weinberg, interrupted mating times.
Solve at least 20 pedigree and 20 mapping problems before the revision phase.

Genes, mutations and complementation: Detecting mutants: replica plating, Ames test, Luria–Delbrück

Mendelian principles and gene interactio: Dihybrid F2 9:3:3:1; recessive epistasis 9:3:4; dominant epistasis 12:3:1; duplicate genes 15:1; complementary genes 9:7.
A recessive lethal gives 2:1 among survivors (yellow mice).
Incomplete dominance gives a 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio.
χ² critical value at p = 0.05 is 3.84 for 1 df and 7.81 for 3 df; df = classes − 1.
Linkage, crossing over and mapping: In a three-point cross the rarest classes are double crossovers; they reveal the middle gene.
Coefficient of coincidence = observed ÷ expected double crossovers; interference = 1 − CoC.
Ordered tetrads: gene–centromere distance = ½ × % second-division segregation.
Bacterial transformation: Griffith (1928): heat-killed S pneumococci transformed live R cells in mice; Avery et al. (1944) showed the agent is DNA.
Naturally competent: Streptococcus pneumoniae (CSP pheromone), Bacillus subtilis, Haemophilus influenzae (needs its uptake sequence).
Only one strand enters a naturally competent cell; RecA integrates it.
Genes close enough to sit on one fragment co-transform often; co-transformation frequency falls with distance.
Conjugation and sexduction: F⁺ × F⁻ makes both cells F⁺; Hfr × F⁻ rarely makes the recipient Hfr because F is transferred last.
Interrupted mating maps genes in minutes; the whole E. coli chromosome takes about 100 min.
Transfer starts at oriT; one strand moves by rolling-circle replication (relaxase TraI).
F′ plasmids carry chromosomal genes, making partial diploids (merodiploids) for complementation tests.
Transduction and phage genetics: Generalised: headful packaging of random host DNA; a P1 particle carries about 100 kb (~2% of the E. coli genome).
Specialised: faulty λ excision carries only gal or bio.
Co-transduction frequency falls as distance rises (Wu formula).
Benzer: rII mutants cannot grow on E. coli K(λ); deletion mapping and cis–trans tests define cistrons.
Genes, mutations and complementation: Transition: purine ↔ purine or pyrimidine ↔ pyrimidine; transversion: purine ↔ pyrimidine.
5-Bromouracil and 2-aminopurine cause transitions; acridines cause frameshifts; EMS alkylates guanine.
Ames test: His⁻ Salmonella reverting on minimal medium, with rat-liver S9 to activate pro-mutagens.
Wild-type phenotype in trans means the two mutations are in different genes (they complement).
Luria–Delbrück fluctuation test: mutations arise before selection; the Poisson P(0) estimates mutation rate.
Sex-linked and extrachromosomal inherita: X-linked recessive: affected sons of carrier mothers, no male-to-male transmission.
Mitochondrial traits pass only through mothers; heteroplasmy gives variable severity (LHON, MELAS).
Maternal effect: offspring phenotype follows the mother’s genotype (snail coiling).
Correns’ Mirabilis jalapa variegation showed maternal plastid inheritance.
Human genetics: LOD = log₁₀(likelihood if linked ÷ likelihood if unlinked); ≥ 3 supports linkage, ≤ −2 rejects it.
Down syndrome is trisomy 21 (mostly maternal meiosis I non-disjunction); Turner 45,X; Klinefelter 47,XXY.
Cystic fibrosis (CFTR ΔF508) is autosomal recessive; Huntington disease (CAG repeat) is autosomal dominant with anticipation.
Mitochondrial pedigrees: all children of an affected mother can be affected, none of an affected father’s.
Population and quantitative genetics: HWE: p² + 2pq + q² = 1; for a rare recessive, carrier frequency ≈ 2q.
X-linked trait: frequency in males = q, in females = q².
Broad-sense H² = VG/VP; narrow-sense h² = VA/VP; response to selection R = h²S.
n additive gene pairs give 2n + 1 phenotypic classes.
Structural and numerical chromosome chan: A crossover in a paracentric inversion loop gives a dicentric bridge and an acentric fragment.
Reciprocal translocation heterozygotes pair as a cross-shaped quadrivalent; adjacent segregation gives unbalanced gametes.
A Robertsonian 14;21 translocation causes familial Down syndrome.

topics: Origin of life and early evolution
Principles of taxonomy and microbial classification

items: Microbial diversity is now inside this unit: bacteria, archaea, viruses, protists and fungi. Give it the most time.
Learn identification keys you can apply: Gram reaction, shape, oxygen needs, IMViC, catalase and oxidase.
Classification by 16S rRNA and genome similarity (ANI) is examined with actual thresholds.
Evolution questions are mostly conceptual; use PYQs to see which mechanisms recur.

Origin of life and early evolution: Three domains and the tree of life
Mechanisms of evolution and speciation: Genetic drift, bottlenecks and founder effects
Adaptive radiation, convergence, coevolution and extinctions
Principles of taxonomy and microbial cla: Molecular methods: 16S rRNA, ANI, DNA–DNA hybridisation
Bacteria: diversity and identification: Biochemical identification and economically important bacteria
Fungi: Fungal pathogens of plants and humans

Origin of life and early evolution: Miller–Urey (1953) made amino acids from CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and H₂O with electric sparks.
Woese used small-subunit rRNA to define Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
Earth is about 4.5 billion years old; stromatolites and microfossils date to about 3.5 billion years.
The Great Oxidation Event, about 2.4 billion years ago, followed oxygenic photosynthesis by cyanobacteria.
Mechanisms of evolution and speciation: Drift is strongest in small populations; the effective population size Ne is usually below the census size.
Allopatric speciation needs geographic separation; sympatric speciation is common in plants through polyploidy.
There have been five mass extinctions; the end-Permian (~252 Ma) was the largest, the end-Cretaceous (~66 Ma) ended non-avian dinosaurs.
Pre-zygotic barriers (habitat, timing, behaviour, mechanical, gametic) act before post-zygotic ones (hybrid inviability, sterility).
Principles of taxonomy and microbial cla: Prokaryotic species: ≥ 70% DNA–DNA hybridisation ≈ ≥ 95–96% average nucleotide identity; 16S rRNA identity below 98.7% suggests a new species.
Bergey’s Manual of Systematics of Archaea and Bacteria is the reference for prokaryote classification.
Within a genus, G + C content (mol%) usually varies by less than 10%.
Binomial names: genus capitalised, species lower-case, both in italics.
Bacteria: diversity and identification: Low G + C Gram-positives: Bacillus, Clostridium, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Lactobacillus; high G + C: Streptomyces, Mycobacterium, Corynebacterium.
Catalase separates Staphylococcus (+) from Streptococcus (−); oxidase separates Pseudomonas (+) from Enterobacteriaceae (−).
Rickettsia and Chlamydia are obligate intracellular parasites; Streptomyces makes about two-thirds of natural antibiotics.
Archaea: Archaea lack peptidoglycan; some methanogens have pseudomurein (N-acetyltalosaminuronic acid, β1→3 links).
Methanogens make CH₄ using coenzyme M and F420 and are strict anaerobes.
Halobacterium uses bacteriorhodopsin as a light-driven proton pump and needs about 3–4 M NaCl.
Archaeal transcription resembles eukaryotic: TBP, TFB and a multi-subunit RNA polymerase.
Pyrolobus fumarii grows at up to 113 °C.
Viruses: structure, replication and impa: Baltimore: I dsDNA; II ssDNA; III dsRNA; IV (+)ssRNA; V (−)ssRNA; VI ssRNA-RT (retroviruses); VII dsDNA-RT (hepadnaviruses).
(−)ssRNA and dsRNA viruses must carry their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion.
One-step growth curve: eclipse, latent period and burst size (T4 about 100–200 per cell).
Viroids are naked circular RNAs of about 250–400 nt (PSTVd); prions are misfolded PrP^Sc.
Plaque assays count infectious virus as plaque-forming units (PFU/mL).
Fungi: Fungal walls contain chitin; the membrane sterol is ergosterol, the target of azoles and amphotericin B.
Ascomycetes make (usually 8) ascospores in an ascus; basidiomycetes make 4 basidiospores on a basidium.
Glomeromycota form arbuscular mycorrhizae with most land plants.
Human pathogens: Candida albicans (dimorphic), Aspergillus fumigatus, Cryptococcus neoformans (capsulated).
Plant pathogens: Magnaporthe oryzae (rice blast), Puccinia (rusts); Phytophthora is an oomycete, not a true fungus.
Protists: Plasmodium: sporozoites from Anopheles → liver → merozoites in red cells; its apicoplast is a relict plastid (a drug target).
Paramecium has a macronucleus (somatic) and micronucleus (germline); conjugation exchanges micronuclei.
Diatoms have silica frustules; dinoflagellates cause red tides.
Dictyostelium aggregates by cAMP signalling; oomycetes have cellulose walls.
Plant life: Bryophytes are gametophyte-dominant and need water for fertilisation.
Ferns are sporophyte-dominant and vascular but seedless; Selaginella is heterosporous.
Gymnosperms have naked seeds and haploid (n) endosperm.
Angiosperms have double fertilisation, triploid endosperm and xylem vessels.
Animal life: Protostomes: blastopore → mouth, spiral determinate cleavage; deuterostomes (echinoderms, chordates): blastopore → anus, radial indeterminate cleavage.
Chordates have a notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits and a post-anal tail.
Protostomes split into Lophotrochozoa (molluscs, annelids) and Ecdysozoa (arthropods, nematodes).
The amniotic egg let reptiles, birds and mammals reproduce away from water.
Human evolution: Homo sapiens arose in Africa about 300,000 years ago (Jebel Irhoud fossils).
Non-African people carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA.
Bipedalism came before large brains (Australopithecus afarensis, ‘Lucy’, ~3.2 Ma).
Most human genetic diversity is within African populations.

Ecological factors and population ecolog: Exponential: dN/dt = rN. Logistic: dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), fastest at N = K/2.
Survivorship: type I (humans), type II (many birds), type III (oysters, most invertebrates).
Levins metapopulation: dp/dt = cp(1 − p) − ep; equilibrium occupancy p* = 1 − e/c.
Community ecology: Gause’s competitive exclusion principle came from Paramecium cultures.
Paine removed Pisaster starfish and showed keystone predation.
Lotka–Volterra equations give coupled predator–prey cycles.
Shannon H′ = −Σ pᵢ ln pᵢ; Simpson D = Σ pᵢ² (diversity = 1 − D).
Ecosystems and biogeochemical cycles: About 10% of energy passes between trophic levels (Lindeman).
The energy pyramid is always upright; the biomass pyramid can be inverted in open-ocean plankton.
Nitrification: Nitrosomonas (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻), Nitrobacter (NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻); anammox bacteria turn NH₄⁺ + NO₂⁻ into N₂.
The phosphorus cycle has no significant gaseous phase.
Human impacts on ecosystems: Atmospheric CO₂ is now above 420 ppm, against about 280 ppm before industrialisation.
Methane traps about 28 times as much heat as CO₂ over 100 years.
Organic pollution raises BOD; eutrophication causes algal blooms and hypoxia.
Lantana camara and water hyacinth are major invasive plants in India.
Biodiversity, conservation and policy: India covers parts of 4 of the 36 global hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats–Sri Lanka and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands).
IUCN threatened categories: Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable.
Biological Diversity Act 2002: National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai), State Biodiversity Boards, Biodiversity Management Committees.
The PPV&FR Act 2001 protects plant varieties and farmers’ rights; the ITPGRFA (2001) covers plant genetic resources for food and agriculture.
Behavioural ecology: Tinbergen’s four questions: mechanism, development, function and evolution.
Hamilton’s rule: altruism spreads when rB > C.
Haplodiploidy makes worker sisters related by r = 0.75 in Hymenoptera.
The honeybee waggle dance codes direction (angle to the sun) and distance (duration of the waggle run).

Biological databases and sequence search: Needleman–Wunsch is global and Smith–Waterman local dynamic-programming alignment.
BLOSUM62 suits moderately divergent proteins; higher BLOSUM numbers are for closer sequences, PAM250 for distant ones.
The E-value is the number of hits expected by chance; lower is more significant.
GenBank, ENA and DDBJ share data daily (INSDC); UniProt holds proteins, PDB structures.
Multiple alignment, phylogenetics and ge: Orthologues diverge by speciation; paralogues by gene duplication.
UPGMA assumes a constant molecular clock; neighbour-joining does not.
Bootstrap support of 70% or more is usually taken as reliable.
Gene finders use ORFs, codon bias and splice signals (GT–AG); Glimmer is built for prokaryotes.
Protein structure prediction and molecul: Homology models are reliable above about 30% sequence identity to the template.
AlphaFold gives a per-residue confidence (pLDDT); above 90 is high confidence.
Force-field energy = bond + angle + torsion + van der Waals + electrostatic terms.
CATH levels: Class, Architecture, Topology, Homologous superfamily.
Drug design and systems biology: Lipinski’s rule of five: MW ≤ 500, logP ≤ 5, ≤ 5 H-bond donors, ≤ 10 acceptors.
Docking ranks ligand poses by a scoring function; virtual screening applies it to whole libraries.
Flux balance analysis models metabolism at steady state from stoichiometry plus constraints.
QSAR relates molecular descriptors to activity by regression.

items: Industrial microbiology lives here: fermentation, sterilisation, antibiotics, bioreactors and downstream processing.
Expect numericals: Monod kinetics, chemostat washout, D- and Z-values, kLa and yields. Practise them with units.
The engineering maths and thermodynamics parts are new; one pass is enough, then drill the fermentation numbers.
Food microbiology is added here for your focus (fermented foods, spoilage, pasteurisation).

Engineering principles for bioprocesses: Calculus and differential equations for growth
Thermodynamics of biological systems: First and second laws in open systems
Media, sterilisation and inoculum: Thermal death kinetics: D, Z and F values
Fermentation products: antibiotics, acid: Citric acid and other organic acids
Vitamins, enzymes, bioplastics and steroid biotransformation
Enzyme technology and immobilisation: Enzymes in organic solvents and ionic liquids
Diffusion limits and the Thiele modulus
Downstream processing, plant design and: Drying, process flow sheets and economics

Engineering principles for bioprocesses: Balance: accumulation = in − out + generation − consumption.
Exponential growth: dX/dt = μX, so X = X₀e^{μt} and doubling time = ln 2/μ.
Pipe flow is laminar when the Reynolds number ρvD/μ is below about 2100.
Thermodynamics of biological systems: Cells are open systems far from equilibrium that continuously produce entropy.
Near equilibrium, fluxes are linear in forces and the cross-coefficients are equal (Onsager reciprocity).
Oxidative phosphorylation captures about 40% of the free energy of glucose oxidation as ATP.
Yeast glycolytic oscillations come from allosteric feedback on PFK, with periods of minutes.
Microbial growth kinetics and bioreactor: Chemostat steady state: μ = D (dilution rate F/V); washout when D exceeds μmax.
Yield Yx/s = ΔX/ΔS; for aerobic growth on glucose it is about 0.5 g/g.
Fed-batch avoids substrate inhibition and overflow metabolism (baker’s yeast, recombinant proteins).
Media, sterilisation and inoculum: D-value: minutes at a set temperature for a 90% kill; Z-value: °C change that alters D tenfold.
Autoclaving: 121 °C, 15 psi, 15–20 min; Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores are the indicator.
Del factor ∇ = ln(N₀/N) sets how long a medium must be sterilised.
Industrial strains are improved by mutagenesis and screening, protoplast fusion and genetic engineering.
Aeration, agitation and scale-up: OTR = kLa(C* − CL); O₂ solubility in water is only about 7–8 mg/L at 25–30 °C.
kLa is measured by the dynamic gassing-out method.
Scale-up keeps one criterion constant (P/V, kLa, tip speed or mixing time); you cannot hold them all.
Filamentous fungal broths are non-Newtonian and pseudoplastic.
Fermentation products: antibiotics, acid: Penicillin: Penicillium chrysogenum (rubens), fed-batch, phenylacetic acid precursor; made in the idiophase.
Citric acid: Aspergillus niger with limited Mn²⁺/Fe and low pH.
Vitamin B12 from Propionibacterium or Pseudomonas denitrificans; riboflavin from Ashbya gossypii.
Cupriavidus necator stores PHB when carbon is in excess and another nutrient is limiting.
Streptomycin comes from Streptomyces griseus; Rhizopus 11α-hydroxylates progesterone.
Food microbiology and fermented foods: Yoghurt: Streptococcus thermophilus with Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus.
Pasteurisation: 63 °C for 30 min (batch) or 72 °C for 15 s (HTST).
Low-acid canning targets Clostridium botulinum with a 12-D process (F₀ ≈ 3 min).
Listeria monocytogenes grows at refrigeration temperatures.
Enzyme technology and immobilisation: Immobilisation: adsorption, covalent binding, entrapment (alginate beads), cross-linking (glutaraldehyde).
Thiele modulus ϕ ≫ 1 means the reaction is diffusion-limited and the effectiveness factor η < 1.
Immobilised glucose isomerase makes high-fructose corn syrup.
Directed evolution (error-prone PCR, DNA shuffling) improves enzymes without needing a structure.
Downstream processing, plant design and: Downstream processing can be 50–80% of production cost.
Proteins are salted out with ammonium sulphate; aqueous two-phase systems use PEG and dextran.
Ultrafiltration separates by molecular-weight cut-off; chromatography by charge, size or affinity.
Artemisinic acid made in engineered yeast is a landmark of synthetic biology.

items: Covers medical, environmental and marine microbiology plus recombinant DNA: core material for your focus.
Vaccines, diagnostics and antimicrobial testing come up often; link them to Unit 4 immunology.
Recombinant DNA questions test vector capacity, selection markers and enzyme specificity.
Environmental biotechnology: wastewater stages, bioremediation organisms and biofertilisers.

Recombinant DNA technology and genome ed: Vectors: plasmids, phage, cosmids, BACs, YACs
Medical biotechnology: vaccines, antibod: Live, killed, subunit, recombinant and nucleic-acid vaccines
Agricultural biotechnology: Gene pyramiding and impact of GE crops
Environmental biotechnology: Biosurfactants and microbially enhanced oil recovery

Recombinant DNA technology and genome ed: Type II restriction enzymes cut inside palindromes (EcoRI: G^AATTC).
Insert capacity: plasmid < 10 kb, λ ~20 kb, cosmid ~45 kb, BAC ~300 kb, YAC ~1 Mb.
Blue–white screening: an insert disrupts lacZα, giving white colonies on X-gal/IPTG.
pET vectors use a T7 promoter in E. coli BL21(DE3).
SpCas9 needs an NGG PAM and makes a blunt cut 3 bp upstream of it.
PCR, sequencing and genome strategies: Taq polymerase lacks 3′→5′ proofreading; Pfu has it.
qPCR: at 100% efficiency the Ct drops by about 3.3 cycles per tenfold more template.
Sanger sequencing uses ddNTPs, which lack a 3′-OH.
Illumina sequences by synthesis with reversible terminators; Nanopore reads long molecules from current changes.
Edman degradation removes residues from the N-terminus with phenylisothiocyanate.
Medical biotechnology: vaccines, antibod: The hepatitis B vaccine (HBsAg made in yeast) was the first recombinant vaccine.
mRNA vaccines use N1-methylpseudouridine-modified mRNA in lipid nanoparticles.
Antibody names: -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, -umab fully human.
CAR-T cells carry an scFv + CD3ζ + a co-stimulatory domain (CD28 or 4-1BB); anti-CD19 CAR-T treats B-cell cancers.
The glucose biosensor uses glucose oxidase.
Stem cells, organoids and clinical micro: Organoids grow from stem cells in Matrigel with niche factors such as Wnt and R-spondin.
Kirby–Bauer disc diffusion uses Mueller–Hinton agar; the MIC is found by broth dilution.
MALDI-TOF identifies microbes from ribosomal-protein mass fingerprints.
Koch’s postulates were updated as molecular Koch’s postulates by Falkow (1988).
Animal biotechnology: Animal cells grow at 37 °C in 5% CO₂ with bicarbonate buffer; serum supplies growth factors.
Primary cells have a finite lifespan; continuous lines such as HeLa and CHO are immortal.
Transgenics are made by pronuclear microinjection, ES-cell targeting or CRISPR in zygotes.
CHO cells are the main host for therapeutic glycoproteins.
Agricultural biotechnology: High auxin:cytokinin gives roots, low gives shoots (Skoog and Miller).
Bt cotton expresses Cry1Ac δ-endotoxin; India approved it in 2002.
Golden Rice makes β-carotene from added psy and crtI genes.
SSR and SNP markers are codominant; RAPD and AFLP are mostly dominant.
Environmental biotechnology: Primary treatment removes solids; secondary (activated sludge, trickling filters) lowers BOD biologically; tertiary removes N and P.
Biogas is about 50–70% CH₄: hydrolysis → acidogenesis → acetogenesis → methanogenesis.
Pseudomonas putida with catabolic plasmids degrades hydrocarbons; Chakrabarty’s strain led to the 1980 patent case.
Biofertilisers: Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum, Anabaena; Bacillus thuringiensis is the leading biopesticide.
Marine biotechnology and biofilms: Prochlorococcus is the most abundant photosynthetic organism in the oceans.
Biofilms embed cells in an EPS matrix and can be up to 1000 times more tolerant of antibiotics.
Sulfate-reducing bacteria (Desulfovibrio) drive microbially influenced corrosion.
Vibrio parahaemolyticus is a major seafood-borne pathogen.
Ziconotide (from a cone snail) and trabectedin (from a tunicate) are marine-derived drugs.

items: Methods questions are reliable marks and Part C loves experimental design: give this unit steady weekly time.
For microbiology add microscopy, staining, culture methods and sterilisation (all included here).
Learn numbers: resolution limits, isotope half-lives, centrifugation formulas, statistical cut-offs.
For each technique know what it measures, its limits, and when to use it instead of the alternatives.

Isolation and separation of macromolecul: Chromatography: ion exchange, gel filtration, affinity, HPLC

Microscopy: Abbe resolution d = 0.61λ/NA; the best light microscopes resolve about 0.2 µm.
Immersion oil (n ≈ 1.515) raises the NA to about 1.4.
Phase contrast shows living unstained cells; confocal uses a pinhole to give optical sections.
TEM needs ultrathin sections (~60–90 nm) stained with heavy metals; SEM images surfaces.
Staining and culture methods: Gram stain: crystal violet → iodine → alcohol → safranin; Gram-positives stay purple.
Ziehl–Neelsen (hot carbol fuchsin) stains mycobacteria red.
Schaeffer–Fulton endospore stain uses malachite green.
MacConkey agar is selective (bile salts, crystal violet) and differential (lactose fermenters pink).
Count plates with 30–300 colonies; CFU/mL = colonies ÷ (dilution × volume plated).
Sterilisation and control of microorgani: Dry heat needs 160–170 °C for about 2 h; filter sterilisation uses 0.22 µm membranes.
The phenol coefficient compares a disinfectant with phenol.
Gamma rays sterilise heat-sensitive disposables; UV (~260 nm) forms thymine dimers but penetrates poorly.
Prions need extended autoclaving at 134 °C or NaOH treatment.
Isolation and separation of macromolecul: Sedimentation coefficients are in Svedberg units (10⁻¹³ s); RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r(cm) × rpm².
SDS-PAGE separates by mass; 2-D gels by pI, then mass.
In gel filtration the largest molecules come out first.
Pulsed-field gels resolve megabase DNA; ordinary agarose about 0.1–25 kb.
Bradford uses Coomassie G-250 at 595 nm; Lowry and BCA rely on Cu⁺.
Biophysical methods and structure determ: CD spectra: α-helix has minima at 208 and 222 nm; β-sheet near 218 nm.
FRET efficiency falls with 1/r⁶ and works over about 1–10 nm.
MALDI-TOF measures intact masses; ESI gives multiply charged ions; MS/MS sequences peptides.
Surface plasmon resonance measures kon, koff and KD without labels.
Molecular biology techniques: Southern = DNA, northern = RNA, western = protein; south-western detects DNA-binding proteins.
DNA barcodes: COI for animals, rbcL and matK for plants, ITS for fungi.
Forensic DNA profiles use STR loci.
RNA-seq expression is reported as TPM or FPKM; differential expression uses fold change and adjusted p-values.
Genomics, proteomics and metabolomics: Yeast two-hybrid tests protein–protein interactions in vivo; co-immunoprecipitation and pull-downs in vitro.
Metagenomics sequences community DNA without culturing; most environmental microbes are not yet culturable.
Bacterial genomes are dense (~88% coding); the human genome is about 1–2% protein-coding.
Untargeted metabolomics uses LC-MS or GC-MS; targeted assays use multiple-reaction monitoring.
Immunotechniques and histochemistry: Sandwich ELISA needs two antibodies to different epitopes; HRP with TMB is read at 450 nm.
Flow cytometry: forward scatter ≈ size, side scatter ≈ granularity.
FISH maps sequences on chromosomes; GISH uses whole genomic DNA to tell parental genomes apart in hybrids.
Immunoprecipitation is greatest at the equivalence zone.
Radiolabelling techniques: Half-lives: ³H 12.3 years, ¹⁴C 5730 years, ³²P 14.3 days, ³⁵S 87 days, ¹²⁵I 60 days.
β-emitters (³H, ¹⁴C, ³²P, ³⁵S) are counted by liquid scintillation; ¹²⁵I by a gamma counter.
Shield ³²P with acrylic, not lead, to avoid bremsstrahlung.
Electrophysiology, imaging and field met: Patch clamp (Neher and Sakmann) records single-channel currents.
fMRI detects the BOLD signal from deoxyhaemoglobin.
Quadrats give density, frequency and abundance of plants.
Statistical methods: Poisson mean = variance = λ, and P(0) = e^{−λ}.
Type I error (α) rejects a true H₀; type II (β) keeps a false one; power = 1 − β.
Standard error = SD/√n; a 95% CI is roughly mean ± 1.96 SE.
Non-parametric tests: Mann–Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal–Wallis.
IPR, biosafety and bioethics: A patent lasts 20 years and needs novelty, an inventive step and industrial applicability.
BSL-1: E. coli K-12; BSL-2: Salmonella, S. aureus; BSL-3: M. tuberculosis; BSL-4: Ebola virus.
India: GEAC (environment ministry) approves environmental release of GMOs, RCGM (DBT) oversees research, IBSCs work in each institution.
Diamond v. Chakrabarty (1980) allowed the first patent on a living engineered microbe.
